slides.title: Who is closest?
slides.transcript: This module answers one question: how much does a pair of circuit cells belong together? We compare three scores: direct edge weight, shared neighbours, and pin-count on multi-pin nets. A score only gives a ranking; it does not decide a grouping. Grouping starts in the next module.

slides.title: The problem
slides.alt: The problem: Input: a weighted undirected graph, or a multi-pin netlist; Output: every positive pair (u, v, score), with u < v; Order: score descending, then u and v alphabetically; Conventions: no self-loops or duplicate edges; a pin repeated in a net counts once; zero pairs are not listed; A score is a ranking
slides.transcript: The input can be a weighted undirected graph or a netlist. The output is the list of every pair with a positive score, each written with u less than v, sorted from the highest score down, with ties by name. This module outputs no groups, and affinity is neither a distance nor a probability.

slides.title: Graphs and nets
slides.alt: Graphs and nets: An ordinary edge connects only two cells; A net can connect the pins of 3, 5 or thousands of cells; Scoring one pair inside a net needs a model first; The clique model: draw the net as pairwise illustrative contributions
slides.transcript: An ordinary edge connects only two cells, but a net can connect many. To score one pair inside a net you first have to choose a model. The common clique model draws the net as pairwise illustrative contributions, but those wires do not really exist.

slides.title: Direct weight and the stable ranking
slides.alt: Direct weight and the stable ranking: edge(u, v) = w(u, v): only directly wired pairs score; G01 has 6 edges, so 6 pairs; A–B and D–E are both 5: by name, A < D; With the tie rule fixed, the ranking does not depend on input order
slides.transcript: The most direct score is the edge weight. G01 has six edges, so six pairs. A–B and D–E are both 5, and by name A comes before D. With a fixed tie rule, the ranking is the same whatever order the edges arrive in.

slides.title: The shared-neighbour score
slides.alt: The shared-neighbour score: shared(u, v) = w(u, v) + Σ_x min(w(u, x), w(v, x)); x is a shared neighbour, connected to both u and v; A link through x is only as strong as its weaker edge: take min; Check every unordered pair: G01 has 10, all positive
slides.transcript: The shared-neighbour score is the direct weight plus the contribution of each shared neighbour, and that contribution takes the smaller of the two edges. Be sure to check every unordered pair: G01 has ten, and all of them score above zero.

slides.title: By hand: A–C and B–D
slides.alt: By hand: A–C and B–D: A–C: direct 1, via B min(5, 4) = 4, total 5; B–D: no direct edge, so the direct part is 0; B–D: via C min(4, 2) = 2, total 2; Score only the existing edges and you miss B–D
slides.transcript: Two pairs by hand. A–C has a direct edge of 1, and the contribution through B is min(5, 4), which is 4, for a total of 5. B and D share no edge, so the direct part is 0; through C they get min(4, 2), which is 2. Compute only on existing edges and you miss B–D.

slides.title: Change the score and the first pair changes
slides.alt: Change the score and the first pair changes: The priority graph (original author Capeur): triangle PQR with every edge 4, X–Y at 5; Direct weight: first pair X–Y @ 5; Shared neighbours: P–Q = 4 + min(4, 4) = 8; P–Q, P–R and Q–R tie at 8; by name, P–Q; X–Y needs 9 to be first again (at 8 it loses the tie to P–Q)
slides.transcript: The original author’s priority graph makes the point well: by direct weight the first pair is X–Y; by shared neighbours, every pair in the triangle gets 4 plus 4, which is 8, and the first pair becomes P–Q. The two scores answer different questions.

slides.title: How wide nets dilute: pin-count
slides.alt: How wide nets dilute: pin-count: Tiny netlist: two five-pin nets connect A–E; the private net n1 connects only E and F; By net count: A–B = 2, E–F = 1; pin-count = Σ w(e) / (|e| − 1); A–B = 1/4 + 1/4 = 0.5; E–F = 1/(2 − 1) = 1; Shared out, the private link E–F comes first
slides.transcript: The original author’s tiny netlist has two wide five-pin nets and one private net. Counting occurrences gives A–B 2 points. pin-count shares each net out over |e| minus 1, so A–B gets only 0.5 while E–F gets 1 and comes first.

slides.title: The pseudocode, line by line
slides.alt: The pseudocode, line by line: Line 1: visit every unordered pair, including pairs with no direct edge; Line 2: with no edge, start from 0; Lines 3–4: add the weaker edge for each shared neighbour; Line 5: record positive scores only (a stated policy); Lines 6–7: stable sort; output the ranking
slides.transcript: Line one visits every unordered pair; line two puts in the direct weight, or 0 with no edge; lines three and four add the weaker edge for each shared neighbour; line five records only positive scores; finally a stable sort, and the ranking is the output.

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.alt: Common mistakes: Shared neighbours on existing edges only: missing B–D and 3 other pairs; Thinking every clustering algorithm merges the top pair first: LP, spectral and KL/FM do not; Not sharing wide nets out: A–B at 2 beats the private E–F; Ties that depend on input order: A–B and D–E swap places; Treating affinit
slides.transcript: Common mistakes: computing shared neighbours on existing edges only; thinking every clustering algorithm merges the top pair first; not sharing wide nets out; letting the input decide the order of ties; and treating affinity as a distance or a probability.

slides.title: Back to the chip: meaning and limits
slides.alt: Back to the chip: meaning and limits: The score decides what gets glued first, which shapes later merging and long cross-region wires; Say where edge weights come from: wire counts, signal importance, or a conversion from nets; The small graphs in this course are invented teaching values, not chip measurements; Shared neighbours check a
slides.transcript: In chip design, the score decides which cells are put together first. Say where edge weights come from. The small graphs in this course are invented teaching values. The shared-neighbour score checks a great many pairs, so large netlists enumerate along adjacency only. And the clique model is only one approximation.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript: In summary: a score gives a ranking and does not decide a grouping, and you should say which model you use. Direct weight looks at how thick one wire is, shared neighbours at whether a pair belongs to a tight little group, and pin-count dilutes wide nets. The next module starts merging for real with the summed weight between clusters.
